title: Why 23 people is enough to share a birthday
description:
In a room of just 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is 50.7%. The trick is counting pairs, not people: 23 people make 253 pairs, and 253 small chances add up fast.

The exact chance nobody matches is 365/365 x 364/365 x ... x 343/365 = 49.3%. Checked by formula and by simulating 200,000 random rooms.
facts_checked: P(shared, n=23) = 1 - prod_{i=0}^{22} (365-i)/365 = 0.5073 (computed); Monte Carlo 200k rooms = 0.5071

beats.say: Only 23 people, and it's better than a coin flip that two of them share a birthday.
That sounds wrong. There are 365 days in a year, and only 23 people.
The mistake is picturing your own birthday. This isn't you against everyone. It's everyone against everyone.
Each pair has only a 1 in 365 chance of matching. But 253 small chances add up fast.
It's easier to find the chance that nobody matches. The second person has to miss the first. The third has to miss both. Keep multiplying.
By the 23rd person, the chance of no match falls below one half. So a shared birthday is more likely than not.
At 50 people it's 97 percent. At 70, it's ninety-nine point nine.
beats.caption: At 50 people it's 97%. At 70, it's 99.9%.

beats.say: A class of 30 has a 71 percent chance. Does yours have a match?
beats.caption: A class of 30 has a 71% chance. Does yours have a match?

angle: count pairs, not people; watch the no-match bar cross one half at the 23rd person
